title: Short Stuff: Neighborhood Watch
summary: Short Stuff episode on Neighborhood Watch. The hosts cover the sign's cartoon burglar mascot (Boris the Burglar), the National Neighborhood Watch Program's founding in 1972 under the National Sheriff's Association after a late-1960s crime rise, and its post-9/11 USA on Watch rebranding funded by a Department of Justice grant that later ran out. They discuss the Chicago School of social disorganization theory, a 2006 review of studies (18 studies, 15 showing crime prevention) on whether watch programs work, and how organizing works, from block captains to police liaisons. They then turn to the risks of vigilantism and profiling, including a Klan-linked watch in Springfield, Missouri, and George Zimmerman and Trayvon Martin in Sanford, Florida in 2012. They close with modern substitutes such as neighborhood text chains, Nextdoor, and Ring doorbell cameras.
topics: Chicago School of social disorganization theory

entities.name: Chicago School of social disorganization theory

segments.title: Opening and the Boris the Burglar sign
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the topic, noting the cartoon burglar on neighborhood watch signs, called Boris the Burglar, and Josh's interest in old signs from the 1970s.

segments.title: History and structure of the National Neighborhood Watch Program
segments.summary: The program was formed officially in 1972 after a rise in late-1960s crime. It operates under the National Sheriff's Association and provides guidelines and pamphlets, but has no direct control over local groups. Josh explains the Chicago School social disorganization theory behind it.
topics: Chicago School of social disorganization theory

segments.title: USA on Watch after 9/11 and the spying era
segments.summary: After 9/11 a Department of Justice grant led the program to rebrand as USA on Watch, adding terrorism to its focus. When the grant ran out it returned to the original name. The hosts describe the period as paranoid.

segments.title: Do neighborhood watches prevent crime?
segments.summary: A 2006 study reviewed 18 other studies, 15 of which suggested watch programs prevent crime, though the programs do not necessarily stop crimes in progress. Proponents say the sign itself deters offenders.

segments.title: How groups are organized
segments.summary: Groups can recruit members, hold meetings, bring in local law enforcement, and have liaisons, coordinators, and block captains. Well-funded groups may run patrols, which can become dodgy.

segments.title: Vigilantism, profiling, and abuses
segments.summary: The hosts discuss watch groups turning vigilante or racially profiling residents. They describe a Springfield, Missouri group that targeted a family, and a Klan-linked watch with signs. Some groups use police scanners and flashing lights.

segments.title: Oversight gap and the Trayvon Martin case
segments.summary: The national association has roughly 28,000 registered groups and limited ability to oversee them. George Zimmerman, described as a neighborhood watch volunteer, killed Trayvon Martin in Sanford, Florida in 2012; the hosts note the group was not an official National Neighborhood Watch group.

segments.title: Modern alternatives: text chains, Nextdoor, Ring
segments.summary: Neighborhood watch activity now happens through text chains, Facebook pages, Nextdoor, and Ring video doorbells, which partner with law enforcement.

segments.title: Starting a registered watch and closing remarks
segments.summary: The hosts advise registering through the National Neighborhood Watch website and doing it the right way, noting people of color are sometimes accosted in their own neighborhoods.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh close the episode with the standard iHeartRadio production credit and podcast availability note.
